**The Practice of Noticing**

There is an hour, just before dawn, when the world seems to hold its breath. I have only met it a handful of times — the hours when I couldn't sleep, or when a flight left too early, or when I stayed up on purpose to see what the night would do with itself. The kitchen is the same kitchen. The window is the same window. But the light is different: not dark, not yet bright, a gray that has a kind of blue in it, like the inside of a shell. The refrigerator hums. A car passes, somewhere, and the sound takes a long time to die. In that hour you can hear the house doing whatever a house does when it thinks no one is listening — the tick of cooling pipes, the settle of old wood, the small electric patience of things waiting to be useful again.

What strikes me, every time, is how much was happening all along. The world did not begin when I turned my attention to it. The sparrows have been up for an hour already, working the hedges. The frost on the window formed itself according to laws I will never understand, in shapes no one will ever see twice. Somewhere a newspaper is being delivered; somewhere a nurse is walking a long corridor; somewhere the sea is doing its eternal arithmetic against the sand. All of this, every night, whether or not anyone is awake to notice it. The world is extravagantly, wastefully full. And most of it goes unwitnessed.

I think about this more than I probably should, because I have come to believe that attention is the one faculty I possess that I use the worst and value the most. Everything I actually remember, everything that feels like it belonged to my life rather than merely happened in it, I remember because at some point I truly looked. And everything else — the commute I cannot recall, the years that collapsed into a single gray length of carpet, the faces of people I must have met a dozen times — those are the products of inattention. A life can be spent in a place and never truly visited.

Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. I used to think that was a beautiful sentence and not much more. Now I think it is a literal description of how love works. To attend to something is to agree, for a moment, to be less important than it. That is a small death of the self, and it is also the only way the self gets larger. The child who crouches on a sidewalk for twenty minutes watching an ant carry a crumb three times its size is practicing something that will matter when the child is grown and sitting across from a frightened friend in a hospital, or standing in a museum in a foreign city, or simply trying to write a sentence that tells the truth. The ant is not the lesson. The crouching is the lesson.

---

I take a walk most mornings, through streets that I have walked so many times I could do it asleep, which is precisely the danger. Familiarity is the anesthetic. The first time I walked this street I noticed everything: the crooked lamppost, the garden gnome with a chipped hat, the way the light came down between the houses at a certain angle around eight o'clock and turned the pavement gold. The hundredth time I noticed the pavement only as something to be avoided, the lamppost only as a landmark meaning *almost home*. The street had not changed. I had closed.

So I have started a small, private discipline, which is to find one thing on every walk that I cannot explain. It is harder than it sounds. Most days the street offers me the same inventory: blackbird, magpie, the smell of bread from the bakery that opens at seven, a man in a green coat walking a dog that is mostly legs. But if I keep looking, the street will eventually produce something. A door I have never seen open, standing open. A bicycle welded into a fence as if it were growing there. A child's glove on a wall, placed carefully, fingers spread, like a small surrendered hand. Once, taped to a lamppost, a piece of paper that said only, in careful capitals, *IF FOUND, PLEASE DO NOT READ.* I stood there for a long time. I did not touch it. I have thought about it nearly every day since. The street has been keeping its secrets for years; it can keep that one.

The point of the discipline is not the finds. The finds are mostly small, and some days there are none. The point is the change in my own machinery — the way, after some weeks of this, I began walking slower without deciding to, the way I began to hear the different sounds of different engines, the way I learned that the blackbird and the thrush do not sing the same song even at a distance, in the dark, when you are sure they do. Attention, it turns out, is not a spotlight. It is more like a muscle, and it has exactly the strength of the use it gets.

---

I want to be fair to distraction, though. It is easy, in an essay like this, to set up a villain, and the villain is always the same villain: the phone, the feed, the glowing rectangle, the great roaring machinery of other people's opinions that we carry in our pockets. I will not pretend I am above it. Some evenings I look up from a screen and an hour has gone somewhere, and I cannot tell you a single thing I saw, because I did not see anything. I was fed. Being fed is not the same as eating.

But distraction is older than the phone. Newton supposedly missed dinner because he was thinking. Every artist in history has been accused, rightly, of not being present at the dinner table, because part of them was in the unfinished thing in the other room. There is a kind of inattention that is actually a deeper attention, aimed at something not yet visible. The writer staring out the window is not wasting the afternoon. She is looking at the inside of a sentence. The distinction, I think, is between attention that is *aimed* and attention that is merely *leaking*. The phone leaks. The daydream that is building something does not. It is the difference between a hole in a bucket and a channel dug on purpose, toward a particular sea.

Still, the leak is real, and I feel it most in the evenings, that strange modern grief of the endless scroll, the sense of having been present for nothing. There is a particular tiredness that comes from that — not the tiredness of work, which has a shape and an end, but the tiredness of a day that never quite happened. I have started to think of those evenings as unlived time. Not wasted, exactly. Unlived. Time that passed through me without leaving a residue, like water through a net.

---

The residue is the whole point, though. Memory is not a camera. It is more like a garden, and attention is the watering of it. Nobody remembers a whole day. What remains are the moments that were truly attended to, and they remain with a strange, unfair vividness. I cannot tell you what I did last Tuesday, but I can tell you about a specific afternoon when I was very small, in a kitchen, watching my grandmother's hands dust flour over a board. I cannot tell you what we said. I can tell you the exact sound the flour made when it left the sieve — not a pour, not a fall, something between, a *hush*, a snowfall in a small warm country. I can tell you that her hands had a map on them that I did not then understand and now, with a jolt, recognize on my own. I was not trying to remember that afternoon. I was simply, for whatever reason, entirely there. Children are like that, when they are not being called in for dinner. Entirely there. It is the great talent we lose and spend our adult lives trying to buy back.

The people I have loved best are the people who made me feel *noticed*, and I can tell you the moment I knew it about each of them. Not the moment I fell in love, particularly — the moment I realized I had been *seen*. A friend who remembered, months later, the name of a book I had mentioned once, in passing, and had forgotten I'd mentioned. A teacher who wrote at the bottom of an essay, not *good work*, but a specific sentence of mine, quoted back to me, with the word *yes* beside it. My mother, at the end of a phone call I made in a bad year, saying: you sound like you're smiling, but it's the kind of smile that's holding something up. I had not said anything was wrong. She had simply been attending, the way you attend to weather, the way you attend to a bird's flight when you are waiting to see where it will land. That is the generosity Weil meant. It costs nothing and it costs everything, and it cannot be faked, and it is the only gift that cannot be returned.

---

Hospitals taught me the rest of it. I have sat in enough of them, in enough chairs of the wrong height, under enough lights that hum, to know that in those rooms attention becomes a moral act with a physical weight. The nurse who looks at the chart and then looks at the patient, and looks long enough that the looking becomes listening, and the listening becomes a kind of knowledge that is not on the chart — that nurse is doing the most human thing there is. And the opposite is also true, and everyone who has waited in those corridors knows the other version: the glance that is already leaving, the question that is not a question, the sense that you have become a task on a list. Nothing cruel was done. Something was merely not attended to. It is the cruelty of absence. It leaves no mark you can point to, and it marks you all the same.

In those chairs I learned that attention is also how we accompany the dying, and that it is one of the few things that survives us in other people. My grandfather, in his last weeks, could not follow a conversation and could not remember the morning. But when someone held his hand and simply stayed, looking at him, not at the window, not at the clock, something in the room changed register. He could not have told you my name on some of those days. He could tell that he was not alone in it. I do not know what a dying person perceives. I know what it looked like from the chair: that being looked at, steadily, without fear, was itself a kind of conversation. We were saying, in the only language left, *you are still a person, and I am still here, and this hour is not elsewhere.*

---

I do not want to end on a dying fall. The practice of noticing is not a preparation for death. It is a practice for mornings, ordinary ones, the ones that will not be remembered and do not need to be. It is the decision, made over and over because it is never made finally, to be in the day rather than near it. Some days I manage it. I see the light do the thing it does between the houses. I hear the flour leave the sieve, in a manner of speaking — some equivalent hush, some small snowfall in some small country. Some days I do not manage it at all, and the day goes through me like water through a net, and I fall asleep having been fed and not having eaten.

But the hour before dawn keeps teaching me the same lesson, whenever I am awake for it. The world does not need my attention in order to continue. The frost will form its impossible letters on the glass whether I read them or not. The sparrows will run their morning economy of hedge and seed. The sea will keep its books. None of it requires me, and that is exactly why attending to it is a gift and not a duty. I am not the sun of this kitchen. I am a guest in it, a guest who is awake, briefly, in the great unending morning of a world that was here before me and will be here after, doing its quiet, extravagant work.

The kettle is starting. The gray at the window is loosening, taking on color. In a few minutes the radio will go on, the day will announce itself in the usual urgent voices, and I will be pulled into the current with everyone else, leaking and aiming, feeding and eating, noticing and not. That is all right. The practice is not a purity. It is a returning. The street will offer me the man in the green coat and the dog that is mostly legs, and if I am lucky it will also offer me something I cannot explain, and if I am wise I will stop and look at it for as long as it takes, which is never very long, and which is always long enough.

Somewhere a nurse is walking a long corridor. Somewhere a child is crouched over an ant. Somewhere a letter writer in an old city is bending over a stranger's words, taking dictation from a heart that cannot spell. The world is full of people paying attention, in the cracks of the day, without calling it anything. It is one of the things the species does. It might be the best thing. And the hour before dawn, when I am lucky enough to be awake in it, is simply the world's way of showing me the work that is always underway, so that I might join it, later, in the daylight, in my own small way: a person at a window, a person on a street, a person across a table, looking — actually looking — at what is there.
